source.title: What Happens During the Loss Plateau? Understanding Abrupt Learning in Transformers

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies abrupt learning and explicitly distinguishes it from grokking, but it does not test the delayed-generalization behavior or mechanisms described by any claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper's small-model experiments use online training with fresh samples at each step; the authors say train and test metrics essentially coincide. They therefore do not measure memorization followed by delayed generalization on a fixed small dataset, or the training-set-size effect in V1. Its attention, repetition, representation, and LLM results concern related training dynamics, not the grokking behavior named by V1–V7. Cited grokking results are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper studies abrupt learning (loss plateau then sudden drop) under online training, where train and test metrics coincide. There is no fixed training set, no memorization phase, no train–test gap and no dataset-size manipulation. The authors explicitly separate this from grokking, calling grokking a fixed-dataset phenomenon. None of V1–V7 is tested. The gradual attention progress before the drop resembles V2's 'hidden progress', but it is for a different phenomenon: abrupt learning, not delayed generalization after memorization.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the plateau co-occurs with a partial solution, repetition bias and representation collapse, and that slow learning of the attention map is a key bottleneck. They report these degenerate patterns in early Pythia/OLMo pretraining, and state that grokking is a distinct fixed-dataset phenomenon.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies online algorithmic-task training and early LLM pretraining dynamics rather than reproducing the fixed-dataset grokking experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Attention-map scaling changes plateau duration, repetition, and representation collapse. The paper also reports changes in abrupt-learning dynamics across initialization scales, optimizers, learning-rate setups, batch sizes, regularization settings, and model configurations; these are not tests of grokking.

fits_no_version.finding: Under online training, attention progress (APM) and probe accuracy increase gradually during the loss plateau, before the abrupt loss drop.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abrupt learning in online Transformer training is preceded by measurable hidden progress in attention maps.

fits_no_version.finding: Abrupt-learning plateaus persist across optimizers (SGD, Muon), linear vs softmax attention, weight decay and initialization scales. Smaller initialization lengthens the plateau.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss plateaus in online algorithmic Transformer training are not optimizer-specific artifacts, and their length depends on initialization scale.

record.problems: The main algorithmic experiments use online training, so train and test metrics essentially coincide and cannot establish a memorization-to-generalization gap. LLM evidence concerns representation similarity and repetition, not delayed generalization. Several comparisons are presented in figures without exact per-condition numerical values; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Other algorithmic-task plots and optimizer, batch-size, regularization, and model-configuration sweeps are not itemized because they report related abrupt-learning dynamics rather than any version's specified grokking behavior.

untested.parts: All parts: fixed small dataset, memorization followed by a delayed generalization jump, and dependence on training-set size. Training is online.
Formation of a generalizing circuit and removal of memorizing components ahead of a grokking jump. The APM and probe progress measures concern online abrupt learning only.
Grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic data and a lazy-to-rich switch. The initialization-scale sweep (Fig 36) alters plateau length in online abrupt learning, not delayed generalization.
Delayed generalization in LLM pretraining or fine-tuning. The Pythia/OLMo results measure only representation collapse and repetition.
Weight-decay efficiency account, critical dataset size, and ungrokking. The weight-decay sweep (Fig 39) concerns online plateaus.
Convergence to the same algorithm across runs.
Optimizer or numerical artifacts causing grokking. Linear attention is used to avoid softmax gradient issues, and plateaus persist under SGD and Muon, but in online abrupt learning, not grokking.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The optimizer, initialization and weight-decay sweeps in Appendix G are left out with justification: they concern online abrupt learning, not grokking. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Fixed small training set, perfect training accuracy with chance test accuracy, delayed test generalization, and the effect of training-set size.
Formation and removal of grokking circuits or memorizing components, and whether such measures anticipate a delayed generalization jump.
Grokking-like delayed generalization on non-algorithmic data and a lazy-to-rich transition. The paper varies initialization and regularization for abrupt learning, not delayed generalization.
Delayed generalization during LLM pretraining or fine-tuning. The LLM experiments measure repetition and representation similarity, not delayed generalization.
Whether low-norm bias favors an efficient generalizing circuit, or predicts critical dataset size and ungrokking.
Whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
Whether grokking is caused by optimizer or numerical artifacts and disappears when those are controlled.

rows.subject: 1-layer, 1-head Transformer (MWS)
rows.operation_detail: Measured training loss and output accuracy during online training

conditions.value: online; fresh batch of 256 samples each step
Adam, learning rate 10^-4, no weight decay

rows.measure: Training loss and output accuracy over steps
rows.value: The loss remains at a sub-optimal value for a significant number of steps, then decreases rapidly; accuracy rises similarly rapidly. Train and test metrics are described as near-identical in this setup.
rows.note: This is abrupt learning in an online setup, not a fixed-dataset overfitting-to-generalization trajectory.

rows.subject: 1-layer, 1-head Transformer (MWS)
rows.operation_detail: Measured frequency of adjacent repeated output tokens
rows.value: Rises to approximately 0.8 in the first approximately 50 steps, then decreases as performance improves.
rows.note: Related training-dynamics result; it does not measure grokking.

rows.subject: 1-layer, 1-head Transformer (MWS)
rows.operation_detail: Measured pairwise cosine similarity between output-position hidden states
rows.value: Rises to approximately 0.95 early in training.
rows.note: The authors report that similarity later drops as performance improves.

rows.subject: 1-layer, 1-head Transformer (MWS)
rows.operation_detail: Measured attention progress toward the task's optimal attention pattern
rows.value: Increases gradually to near 0.8, with nontrivial increase during the loss plateau and before the sudden loss drop.
rows.note: This measures progress toward the task's attention pattern, not a grokking circuit.

rows.subject: 1-layer, 1-head Transformer (MWS)
rows.operation_detail: Multiplied attention scores at optimal positions by c=10 from the start of training
rows.measure: Loss convergence, hidden-state cosine similarity, and repetition frequency
rows.baseline: Unscaled attention map, c=1; peak cosine similarity approximately 0.95
rows.value: Peak cosine similarity approximately 0.6, for a negligible duration compared with c=1; the model converges faster, with lower repetition frequency.
rows.locator: Section 4, Biasing the Attention Map; Figures 3 and 43
rows.note: A direct attention intervention changes abrupt-learning dynamics; it does not test delayed generalization.

rows.subject: 1-layer, 1-head Transformer (MWS)
rows.operation_detail: Scaled attention scores at optimal positions downward
rows.measure: Loss convergence, hidden-state cosine similarity, and repetition frequency
rows.value: The model takes much longer to converge and remains in a representation-collapse and high-repetition state longer than with c=1.
rows.locator: Section 4, Biasing the Attention Map; Figure 4
rows.note: The paper describes the two c settings together rather than giving separate numerical outcomes.

rows.subject: 1-layer, 1-head Transformer (MWS)
rows.operation_detail: Initialized attention-related components to final values from a normal run and trained subsequent non-fixed layers

conditions.value: embeddings, attention LayerNorm, and attention weights; either K,Q or K,Q,V,O

rows.measure: Time to convergence, loss plateau, representation cosine similarity, and repetition
rows.value: Both attention-initialized cases converge significantly faster, without significant representation collapse, repetitions, or loss plateau. Including V,O gives a peak average cosine similarity of approximately 0.15 rather than approximately 0.45 for K,Q alone.
rows.locator: Section 4, Training with Optimal Attention Map v. Other Components; Figure 5
rows.note: The authors report a separate comparison between initializing K,Q and initializing K,Q,V,O.

rows.subject: 1-layer, 1-head Transformer (MWS)
rows.operation_detail: Fixed optimal MLP or embeddings together with LM head, then retrained other components

conditions.value: MLP or embeddings plus LM head

rows.measure: Loss plateau, repetition, and representation collapse
rows.value: Training dynamics do not qualitatively change; a significant loss plateau, repetition bias, and representation collapse still occur.
rows.locator: Section 4, Training with Optimal Attention Map v. Other Components; Figure 5
